items.good: The document follows the template from the top: the title '# tidy-downloads architecture', an opening sentence on how the tool is put together with a link to docs/ux.md, then the principles. Line 10 says it is built on nothing but Python 3, so there are no principles of a base to link to. Then come '## User stories', '## Architecture' with '### Logical view' (one mermaid figure, each box holding a name only, each arrow labelled) and '### Physical view' (a text tree with what each part is made of, then the dependencies and how it is started), and '## Test'. The Test section has no link, and line 94 says why: the project has no test rules apart from that section. That matches the user's decision in commit c169342. Each list line is one sentence, with its why indented under it after a blank line. Nothing is in bold.

From the opening I can tell how the tool is put together: one Python 3 script, run in a terminal, that sorts the files directly in the folder into the folder of each one's kind, and keeps a hidden record of the last move in that folder so an undo can work. The opening links the UX terms. Line 10 says the tool is built on nothing but Python 3, so every principle is its own. There are three principles, each one line with its why: only the Mover moves files and makes or removes folders, and only to an empty path, which it checks at each file; the tool keeps its memory inside the folder it sorts; the tool is whole in one file. Each of these is a ground I can hold later lines to, not a tool or a format.

I matched each UX scene in docs/ux.md to a story. 'Seeing what would move' rests on the preview story, 'Moving' on the move story and 'Undoing' on the undo story. 'The whole way' is those three in turn. Each story is one command the user runs at the tool's edge. None is a step inside the tool, none repeats another, and none is named after Python.

From the figure and the lines under it, with the Mover's check in the principle at lines 12-13, I can follow each story in order. Preview: the Command asks the Sorter, the Sorter lists the Folder, and the plan is printed; the Mover is never reached (line 50). Move: the Command hands the Sorter's plan to the Mover. The Mover checks the path and moves each file, making the folder of its kind if needed. It starts a new record with the first file moved and notes each file, and the Command prints what the Mover reports (lines 51-57). The Sorter leaves out the record's own file (line 59). Undo: the Command reads the record and hands the Mover each file to go back, without the Sorter. The Mover then removes each empty folder of a kind that the last move made, and the Command clears the record (lines 63-72). Each choice a reader would question has its why. Each box holds a name only, and no path serves one case alone.

The tree places Command, Sorter and Mover in the one Python 3 script 'tidy-downloads' at the root of the repository, the tests in tests/test_tidy_downloads.py as Python 3 unittest tests, and the Record as the JSON file .tidy-downloads-last in the folder the tool is run on. Each place has its kind beside it. Lines 85-88 say what the tool depends on (Python 3 and its standard library, on macOS or Linux, with python3 found on the PATH) and how it is started (as the command 'tidy-downloads', once copied onto the PATH). I checked the link ../README.md#installation: README.md has '## Installation'.

Line 94 says the project has no test rules apart from this section, which is the user's decision in commit c169342, so I know there is nothing elsewhere to follow. For the script and the user stories, the rule is tests in tests/, each a Given, a When and a Then, that run the script as the user does on a temporary folder, never the real Downloads folder. For each component, the rule is the runs of the stories it serves. A run with no folder named points HOME at a temporary folder. The tests run on both macOS and Linux. No case's inputs or pass bar are written here beyond what the rule needs.

I held each arrow and line against the three principles. Only the Mover's arrows move a file or make or remove a folder. The Command only reads and clears the Record, and the Sorter only lists the Folder. The Mover makes its check at each file (line 13), including the files an undo hands it (line 63). The record is only ever in the sorted folder (line 82), and only the standard library is used (line 85). No two lines ask for opposite things. A move that moves no file leaves the record as it was, the undo clears it after one run, and an empty folder made by the last move is removed while one holding a file stays. These hold together, and they match the README's example.

Each decision is now said once. The Mover's check, and that every file a move or an undo moves passes through it, is only in the principle (lines 12-17). That an undo never asks the Sorter is only at line 63. JSON as the record's format is only in the tree (line 82), and line 89 gives only its why. Every other line is a decision the approval rests on, such as where the record is, when a new record starts, and what an undo removes. No line tells how a part behaves step by step, and none gives history or status.

Lines 7-8 say that a move is always a run, as the UX defines it, and that a single file going into another folder is said as moving a file. Every use since holds to this, and I read each one right the first time: 'Every file a move or an undo moves' (line 15), 'hands each file to move' (line 44), 'notes each file moved' (line 46), 'the first file a move moves' (line 53), 'A move that moves no file' (line 56). The UX terms are linked from the opening. Mover is met at line 12 with what it does. Each other component name is used for one thing only, and no line rests on a reason given later.
